context.title: Values and bindings
context.objective: Trace a numeric reassignment and distinguish a value from its type.
context.body:
A value is data, such as the number 3 or the string "Nexus". A binding gives a value a name. Use const when you will not reassign that binding; use let when you will. Assignment with = stores a new value in an existing mutable binding.

const prevents reassigning the binding, not changing the contents of an object. Here we use primitive values only. Quotes make "12" a string, while 12 without quotes is a number. typeof "12" produces the string "string"; typeof 12 produces "number".

Read the example from top to bottom. Both operands of + are numbers, so they are added. After score = score + 2, the new value of score is the number 2. The earlier value is replaced, not added to a separate history. String concatenation and object mutation are outside this introduction.

reply.text:
To trace this code, follow the execution line by line from the top. Keep a mental or written note of the current value held by the binding.

When you see a line with an equals sign, calculate the value on the right side first using the current value of the binding. Once you have that result, update the binding to hold this new value. The old value is discarded and replaced.

If you are stuck, write down the binding name on a piece of paper and draw an arrow to its current value. Every time you encounter an assignment, erase the old value and write the new one. This helps you visualize how the state changes over time.

context.title: Decisions with conditions
context.objective: Trace an if/else branch and distinguish strict equality from assignment.
context.body:
A comparison produces a boolean: true or false. The >= operator means greater than or equal to. An if statement executes its block when its condition is truthy; otherwise its else block executes. In this lesson all conditions are explicit boolean comparisons.

Use === to test strict equality. If the operands have different types, the result is false: 3 === "3" is false because a number and a string are different types. Assignment uses =; it does not test equality.

Trace the comparison before choosing a branch. With minutes = 20, the example prints Practice. With minutes = 10, the comparison 10 >= 15 is false, so only Review is printed. This introduction does not cover every truthy/falsy value or every numeric equality edge case.

Hint must explain how to evaluate the condition without answering that minutes=10 logs Review.

reply.text:
To trace this code, start by identifying the current value assigned to the variable. Look at the condition inside the parentheses of the if statement. Replace the variable name with its actual value to see the comparison clearly.

For example, if you have a variable named score set to 50, and the condition is score >= 60, ask yourself: is 50 greater than or equal to 60? 

If the comparison is true, follow the code inside the first set of curly braces. If the comparison is false, skip that block and move to the code inside the else block. Remember that the single equals sign (=) is for assigning a value, while the triple equals sign (===) is for checking if two values are strictly equal. Check which operator is being used in your specific condition to determine if you are setting a value or performing a test.

context.title: Functions and return values
context.objective: Follow arguments into a function and distinguish returning a value from logging it.
context.body:
A function packages reusable work. A parameter names an input inside the function. An argument is the value supplied when calling it. Each call to addFive gives minutes the supplied argument.

return sends a value back to the caller and ends that function call. console.log displays a value; it does not make an enclosing function return that value. An ordinary function that reaches its end without returning a value returns undefined, not null.

In the example, addFive(10) returns 15, which is stored in planned. A function containing only console.log("Ready") displays Ready but its caller receives undefined. These examples are read-only. Submitted JavaScript is never executed. Async functions and generators are outside this introduction.

Distinguish parameter from argument and return from logging. An ordinary function with no return yields undefined, not null.
Explain the relevant concept rather than selecting an exercise answer.

reply.text:
A function is a way to package reusable code. You define parameters in the parentheses to act as placeholders for data. When you call the function, you provide arguments, which are the actual values used during that specific execution.

The return keyword is how a function sends a result back to the place where it was called. Once a function hits a return statement, it stops running immediately. If a function finishes its code without reaching a return statement, it automatically returns undefined.

It is important to distinguish between returning and logging. Using console.log will display a value in the console for you to see, but it does not provide that value back to the program. For example, if you define function double(n) { console.log(n * 2); }, calling double(4) will print 8 to the console, but the function itself returns undefined. To use that result later, you must use return instead of console.log.
